items.title: Quiz Q#90 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson

Which of the following works were written by James Thomson?

items.title: Quiz Q#91 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin

Which of the following works were written by Benjamin Franklin?

(C) Experiments and Observations on Electricity
(D) Common Sense
items.explanation: The Autobiography, Poor Richard’s Almanack, and Experiments and Observations on Electricity are works by Benjamin Franklin, whereas 'Common Sense' was written by Thomas Paine.

items.title: Quiz Q#92 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding

Which of the following works were written by Henry Fielding?

items.title: Quiz Q#93 · Samuel Johnson

items.title: Quiz Q#94 · David Hume
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · David Hume

items.title: Quiz Q#95 · Thomas Gray

Which of the following works were written by Thomas Gray?
(A) Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
(B) The Progress of Poesy

items.title: Quiz Q#96 · Hugh Blair
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Hugh Blair

(D) Elements of Criticism
items.explanation: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, the Critical Dissertation on Ossian, and Sermons were authored by Hugh Blair, whereas 'Elements of Criticism' was written by Henry Home, Lord Kames.

items.title: Quiz Q#97 · Tobias Smollett
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Tobias Smollett
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Tobias Smollett?
(A) The Expedition of Humphry Clinker
(B) The Adventures of Roderick Random
(C) The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle
(D) A Sentimental Journey
items.explanation: Humphry Clinker, Roderick Random, and Peregrine Pickle are picaresque and epistolary novels by Tobias Smollett, whereas 'A Sentimental Journey' was authored by Laurence Sterne.

items.title: Quiz Q#98 · William Collins
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Collins
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by William Collins?
(A) Ode to Evening
(B) The Passions: An Ode for Music
(C) Ode on the Poetical Character
(D) The Deserted Village
items.explanation: Ode to Evening, The Passions, and Ode on the Poetical Character are lyric odes by William Collins, whereas 'The Deserted Village' was composed by Oliver Goldsmith.

items.title: Quiz Q#99 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Oliver Goldsmith?
(A) The Vicar of Wakefield
(B) The Traveller
(C) The Deserted Village
(D) The Citizen of the World was composed by Samuel Johnson
items.explanation: The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), The Traveller (1764), and The Deserted Village (1770) were all authored by Oliver Goldsmith. The Citizen of the World (1762) was also written by Goldsmith (Lien Chi Altangi letters), not Johnson.

items.title: Quiz Q#100 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by William Cowper?
(A) The Task
(B) The Castaway
(C) The Diverting History of John Gilpin
(D) The Village
items.explanation: The Task, The Castaway, and John Gilpin are famous poems by William Cowper, whereas 'The Village' was authored by George Crabbe.

items.title: Quiz Q#101 · Thomas Paine
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Paine
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Thomas Paine?
(A) Common Sense
(B) Rights of Man
(C) The Age of Reason
(D) Reflections on the Revolution in France
items.explanation: Common Sense, Rights of Man, and The Age of Reason were written by Thomas Paine, whereas 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' was authored by Edmund Burke.

items.title: Quiz Q#102 · Richard Brinsley Sheridan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Richard Brinsley Sheridan
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Richard Brinsley Sheridan?
(A) The Rivals
(B) The School for Scandal
(C) The Critic
(D) She Stoops to Conquer
items.explanation: The Rivals, The School for Scandal, and The Critic are major comedies by Richard Brinsley Sheridan, whereas 'She Stoops to Conquer' was written by Oliver Goldsmith.

items.title: Quiz Q#103 · Fanny Burney
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Fanny Burney
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Fanny Burney?
(A) Evelina
(B) Cecilia
(C) Camilla
(D) The Mysteries of Udolpho
items.explanation: Evelina, Cecilia, and Camilla are novels of manners by Fanny Burney, whereas 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' was written by Ann Radcliffe.

items.title: Quiz Q#104 · Thomas Chatterton
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Chatterton
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Thomas Chatterton?
(A) Poems, Supposed to Have Been Written at Bristol, by Thomas Rowley
(B) The Execution of Sir Charles Bawdin
(C) An Ella; a Tragycal Enterlude
(D) The Castle of Otranto
items.explanation: The Rowley Poems, Sir Charles Bawdin, and Ella are pseudo-medieval works forged by Thomas Chatterton, whereas 'The Castle of Otranto' was written by Horace Walpole.

items.title: Quiz Q#105 · William Godwin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Godwin
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by William Godwin?
(A) Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams
(B) An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice
(C) St. Leon
(D) The Monk
items.explanation: Caleb Williams, Political Justice, and St. Leon are major works by William Godwin, whereas 'The Monk' was authored by Matthew Gregory Lewis.

items.title: Quiz Q#106 · William Blake
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Blake
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by William Blake?
(A) Songs of Innocence
(B) The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
(C) Songs of Experience
(D) Lyrical Ballads
items.explanation: Songs of Innocence, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and Songs of Experience were created by William Blake, whereas 'Lyrical Ballads' was co-authored by Wordsworth and Coleridge.

items.title: Quiz Q#107 · Mary Wollstonecraft
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Mary Wollstonecraft

(C) Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman
(D) A Simple Story
items.explanation: A Vindication of the Rights of Men, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, and Maria were written by Mary Wollstonecraft, whereas 'A Simple Story' was authored by Elizabeth Inchbald.

items.title: Quiz Q#108 · Robert Burns
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Robert Burns

Which of the following works were written by Robert Burns?
(A) Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect
(B) Tam o’ Shanter
(C) The Cotter’s Saturday Night
(D) The Minstrel
items.explanation: Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect, Tam o’ Shanter, and The Cotter’s Saturday Night are works by Robert Burns, whereas 'The Minstrel' was composed by James Beattie.

items.title: Quiz Q#109 · Ann Radcliffe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Ann Radcliffe

Which of the following works were written by Ann Radcliffe?

(D) The Monk
items.explanation: The Romance of the Forest, The Mysteries of Udolpho, and The Italian are Gothic romances by Ann Radcliffe, whereas 'The Monk' was written by Matthew Gregory Lewis.

items.title: Quiz Q#110 · Thomas Parnell
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Parnell
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Thomas Parnell?
(A) A Night-Piece on Death
(B) The Hermit

(D) The Grave
items.explanation: A Night-Piece on Death, The Hermit, and An Elegy to an Old Beauty are poems by Thomas Parnell, whereas 'The Grave' was composed by Robert Blair.

items.title: Quiz Q#111 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Bunyan:
Statement I: John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress' (Part I, 1678) is a foundational spiritual allegory composed as a dream vision depicting Christian's journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City.
Statement II: In 'The Holy War' (1682), Bunyan allegorizes human salvation and spiritual warfare through the siege and defense of the metaphorical town of Mansoul.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. John Bunyan composed 'The Pilgrim's Progress' (1678) largely while imprisoned in Bedford gaol, and followed it with 'The Holy War' (1682), using detailed allegories of Christian spiritual struggle.

items.title: Quiz Q#112 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Dryden:
Statement I: John Dryden's 'An Essay of Dramatic Poesy' (1668) is a critical dialogue debating the relative merits of classical, modern, French, and English drama.
Statement II: In the essay, the persona of Neander represents Dryden himself and offers a celebrated defense of English drama, praising William Shakespeare and Ben Jonson.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Published in 1668, Dryden's 'An Essay of Dramatic Poesy' employs four speakers (Crites, Eugenius, Lisideius, and Neander), with Neander famously championing Shakespeare as having the 'most comprehensive soul'.

items.title: Quiz Q#113 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Locke:
Statement I: In 'A Letter Concerning Toleration' (1689), John Locke argues that the civil magistrate's power is strictly confined to civil interests and cannot coerce religious conscience.
Statement II: Locke's 'An Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) rejects Cartesian innate ideas, famously positing the mind at birth as a 'tabula rasa' or white paper.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. John Locke published both foundational texts in 1689, establishing the philosophical principles of religious toleration and empirical epistemology.

items.title: Quiz Q#114 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Aphra Behn:
Statement I: Aphra Behn's epistolary novel 'Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister' (1684) is among the earliest works of psychological prose fiction in English literature.
Statement II: Her celebrated comedy 'The Rover' (1677) centers on the banished English cavalier Captain Willmore and the Spanish courtesan Angellica Bianca during Carnival in Naples.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Aphra Behn was England's first professional woman writer, pioneering both the epistolary political roman à clef in 1684 and brilliant Restoration intrigue comedy in 'The Rover' (1677).

items.title: Quiz Q#115 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Wycherley:
Statement I: William Wycherley's 'The Country Wife' (1675) is a satirical comedy of manners featuring Harry Horner's scandalous pretense of impotence to deceive jealous husbands.
Statement II: In 'The Plain Dealer' (1676), Wycherley adapts Molière's 'Le Misanthrope' through the uncompromising honesty of Captain Manly.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Wycherley's 'The Country Wife' (1675) and 'The Plain Dealer' (1676) represent the satirical apex of Restoration stage wit, ruthlessly exposing social hypocrisy.

items.title: Quiz Q#116 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Thomas Otway:
Statement I: Thomas Otway's 'The Orphan' (1680) contributed decisively to the development of domestic she-tragedy by focusing pathos upon the suffering heroine Monimia.
Statement II: Otway's masterpiece 'Venice Preserved' (1682) dramatizes the moral and emotional turmoil of Jaffeir, torn between friendship with Pierre and love for Belvidera.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Otway's blank-verse tragedies 'The Orphan' (1680) and 'Venice Preserved' (1682) moved the Restoration stage away from grand heroic rhymed bombast toward deep domestic and political pathos.

items.title: Quiz Q#117 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Daniel Defoe:
Statement I: Daniel Defoe's 'A Journal of the Plague Year' (1722) employs documentary realism, bills of mortality, and personal anecdote to reconstruct the 1665 London epidemic.
Statement II: In the satirical pamphlet 'The Shortest Way with the Dissenters' (1702), Defoe adopted an ironic High Church Tory persona that led to his arrest and imprisonment.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Defoe demonstrated masterful mastery of ironic pamphleteering in 1702 and pioneered realistic historical journalism in 'A Journal of the Plague Year' (1722).

items.title: Quiz Q#118 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Vanbrugh:
Statement I: Sir John Vanbrugh wrote 'The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger' (1696) as a witty, skeptical sequel to Colley Cibber's sentimental comedy 'Love's Last Shift'.
Statement II: In 'The Provoked Wife' (1697), Vanbrugh examined marital incompatibility and domestic misery through the abusive husband Sir John Brute.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Vanbrugh's comedies challenged sentimental pieties and provoked fierce denunciations from moralist reformer Jeremy Collier in 1698.

items.title: Quiz Q#119 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Matthew Prior:
Statement I: Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu co-authored 'The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd' (1687) as a verse parody of John Dryden's Catholic beast fable.
Statement II: Prior's 'Poems on Several Occasions' (1709/1718) established him as one of the preeminent Augustan masters of polished society verse and light epigram.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Matthew Prior began his literary fame by burlesquing Dryden's apologetics with the Country Mouse and City Mouse in 1687, later perfecting elegant Augustan occasional verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#120 · Jonathan Swift
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Jonathan Swift
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Jonathan Swift:
Statement I: Jonathan Swift's 'The Battle of the Books' (1704) is a mock-heroic prose satire defending ancient literature against modern pretensions, introducing the debate of the Spider and the Bee.
Statement II: In 'A Tale of a Tub' (1704), Swift allegorizes the divisions of Western Christianity through the three brothers Peter, Martin, and Jack, amidst wild satirical digressions.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Swift published both masterpieces together in 1704, defending classical antiquity and lampooning religious fanaticism and pedantic scholarship.

items.title: Quiz Q#121 · William Congreve
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Congreve
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Congreve:
Statement I: William Congreve's theatrical debut 'The Old Bachelor' (1693) was staged with great commercial success under the enthusiastic sponsorship of John Dryden.
Statement II: In 'Love for Love' (1695), the protagonist Valentine Legend feigns madness to escape his creditors and preserve his inheritance for his beloved Angelica.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Congreve achieved instant acclaim with 'The Old Bachelor' in 1693 and solidified his dramatic reputation with 'Love for Love' (1695) at Lincoln's Inn Fields.

items.title: Quiz Q#122 · Colley Cibber
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Colley Cibber
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Colley Cibber:
Statement I: Colley Cibber's 'Love's Last Shift' (1696) is widely credited with inaugurating the tradition of 18th-century sentimental comedy through the moral reformation of Loveless.
Statement II: In 'The Careless Husband' (1704), Cibber dramatizes gentle marital reconciliation, notably in the famous 'Steinkirk scene' involving Lady Easy's lace kerchief.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Cibber shifted English stage comedy from cynical Restoration libertinism toward moral sentiment and domestic reform in both 1696 and 1704.

items.title: Quiz Q#123 · Joseph Addison
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Joseph Addison
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Joseph Addison:
Statement I: Joseph Addison's eleven essays on the 'Pleasures of the Imagination' (The Spectator, 1712) established foundational psychological principles for 18th-century aesthetics.
Statement II: 'The Spectator' (1711–1712), founded by Addison and Richard Steele, created the beloved gentlemanly persona of Sir Roger de Coverley to illustrate countryside manners.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Addison's 'Spectator' essays pioneered both modern literary aesthetic theory and genial social satire through the fictional members of the Spectator Club.

items.title: Quiz Q#124 · Richard Steele
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Richard Steele
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Richard Steele:
Statement I: Richard Steele launched 'The Tatler' in April 1709, adopting Jonathan Swift's satirical pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff to report coffeehouse news and moral reflection.
Statement II: In 'The Conscious Lovers' (1722), Steele achieved the quintessential expression of sentimental comedy, prioritizing moral tears and filial benevolence over satirical laughter.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Steele pioneered the popular periodical essay in 'The Tatler' (1709) and later codified the conventions of high sentimental drama in 'The Conscious Lovers' (1722).

items.title: Quiz Q#125 · Nicholas Rowe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Nicholas Rowe
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Nicholas Rowe:
Statement I: Nicholas Rowe's blank-verse tragedy 'The Fair Penitent' (1703) introduced the archetype of the aristocratic libertine seducer, 'the gallant, gay Lothario'.
Statement II: In 'Jane Shore' (1714), Rowe composed a historical she-tragedy 'in imitation of Shakespeare's style', dramatizing the pathetic public penance of King Edward IV's mistress.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Rowe was the leading Augustan tragic dramatist and the first formal editor of Shakespeare's dramatic works (1709), popularizing pathetic she-tragedies.

items.title: Quiz Q#126 · George Farquhar
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · George Farquhar
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding George Farquhar:
Statement I: George Farquhar's 'The Recruiting Officer' (1706) drew upon his own military service in Shropshire to portray provincial English life, Captain Plume, and Sergeant Kite.
Statement II: 'The Beaux' Stratagem' (1707), written on Farquhar's deathbed, advocated legal divorce for marital incompatibility while depicting Aimwell and Archer hunting heiresses.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Farquhar revitalized late Restoration comedy by moving the action out of aristocratic London drawing rooms into lively provincial towns and coaching inns.

items.title: Quiz Q#127 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Gay:
Statement I: John Gay's 'The Shepherd's Week' (1714) is a sequence of six rustic pastorals in heroic couplets that parodied Ambrose Philips by presenting realistic English farm customs.
Statement II: Gay's 'Trivia; or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London' (1716) is a mock-georgic poem in heroic couplets offering practical advice against urban London hazards.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Gay demonstrated brilliant versatility in applying classical genres (pastoral and georgic) to contemporary English rural and street settings.

items.title: Quiz Q#128 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Alexander Pope:
Statement I: Alexander Pope's 'An Essay on Criticism' (1711) is a didactic poem in heroic couplets articulating Neoclassical critical doctrines and advising critics to 'follow Nature'.
Statement II: In 'An Essay on Man' (1733–1734), Pope constructs a philosophical theodicy in four epistles, famously concluding with the affirmation that 'Whatever is, is right'.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Pope's heroic couplets set the gold standard for Augustan didactic and philosophical verse, synthesizing classical aesthetics and Enlightenment rationalism.

items.title: Quiz Q#129 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Samuel Richardson:
Statement I: Samuel Richardson's epistolary novel 'Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded' (1740) revolutionized English fiction through its minute psychological technique of 'writing to the moment'.
Statement II: In 'Clarissa' (1747–1748), Richardson created an epic epistolary tragedy depicting the moral struggle between the virtuous heroine Clarissa Harlowe and the libertine Lovelace.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Richardson's epistolary novels established psychological realism and intense moral introspection as hallmarks of the developing English novel.

items.title: Quiz Q#130 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Anne Finch:
Statement I: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea, composed 'A Nocturnal Reverie' (1713), a nature poem in heroic couplets praised by Wordsworth for its delicate nocturnal imagery.
Statement II: Her Pindaric ode 'The Spleen' (1701) provides an incisive poetic analysis of female depression, melancholy, and creative anxiety in the early 18th century.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Anne Finch was one of the most distinctive Augustan poets, celebrated for her genuine observation of natural phenomena and perceptive psychological verses.

items.title: Quiz Q#131 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding James Thomson:
Statement I: James Thomson's blank-verse descriptive poem 'The Seasons' (1726–1730) played a monumental role in shifting British poetry from urban satire back to external nature.
Statement II: In 'The Castle of Indolence' (1748), Thomson employed the Spenserian stanza to create an allegorical contrast between luxurious languor and energetic industry.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. James Thomson helped inspire the pre-Romantic movement through his grand Miltonic blank verse in 'The Seasons' and exquisite Spenserian imitation in 1748.

items.title: Quiz Q#132 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Benjamin Franklin:
Statement I: Benjamin Franklin's 'Autobiography' (begun in 1771) established the classic American archetype of the self-made individual through an explicit scheme of 13 moral virtues.
Statement II: His annual 'Poor Richard's Almanack' (1732–1758), published under the persona of Richard Saunders, popularized hundreds of maxims on industry, thrift, and prudence.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Franklin's writings embodied Enlightenment pragmatism, civic self-improvement, and colonial American secular wisdom.

items.title: Quiz Q#133 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Henry Fielding:

Both Statement I and Statement II are true

items.title: Quiz Q#134 · Samuel Johnson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Samuel Johnson:
Statement I: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language' (1755) standardized English lexicography with over 40,000 definitions illustrated by over 114,000 literary quotations.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

items.title: Quiz Q#135 · David Hume
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · David Hume
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding David Hume:
Statement I: David Hume's 'A Treatise of Human Nature' (1739–1740) sought to introduce the experimental method of reasoning into moral subjects, challenging rationalist theories of causation.
Statement II: In 'An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding' (1748), Hume formulated his celebrated philosophical argument against the evidential credibility of religious miracles.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. David Hume's radical empirical skepticism reshaped modern epistemology, ethics, and the philosophy of religion.

items.title: Quiz Q#136 · Laurence Sterne
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Laurence Sterne
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Laurence Sterne:
Statement I: Laurence Sterne's 'Tristram Shandy' (1759–1767) subverts traditional chronological storytelling through Lockeian associations of ideas, eccentric digressions, and visual gimmicks.
Statement II: In 'A Sentimental Journey' (1768), Sterne used the traveler Mr. Yorick to emphasize subjective emotional sensibility, delicacy of feeling, and benevolence.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Laurence Sterne pioneered experimental metafiction in 'Tristram Shandy' and refined the 18th-century Cult of Sensibility in 'A Sentimental Journey'.

items.title: Quiz Q#137 · Thomas Gray
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Gray
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Thomas Gray:
Statement I: Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751) is composed in heroic quatrains (abab) and stands as the supreme masterpiece of Graveyard poetry.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Thomas Gray was the foremost poetic craftsman of the mid-18th century, transitioning from reflective Graveyard meditation to sublime antiquarian lyricism.

items.title: Quiz Q#138 · Hugh Blair
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Hugh Blair

Given below are two statements regarding Hugh Blair:

Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

items.title: Quiz Q#139 · Tobias Smollett
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Tobias Smollett
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Tobias Smollett:
Statement I: Tobias Smollett's 'The Expedition of Humphry Clinker' (1771) is a polyphonic epistolary novel depicting a family's travels across England and Scotland through five distinct letter-writers.
Statement II: Smollett's picaresque novels 'Roderick Random' (1748) and 'Peregrine Pickle' (1751) draw upon naval experiences to capture vibrant nautical caricatures like Lieutenant Bowling and Commodore Trunnion.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Tobias Smollett was a master of robust satirical realism, picaresque naval adventure, and multi-perspective epistolary comedy.

items.title: Quiz Q#140 · William Collins
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Collins
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Collins:
Statement I: William Collins's 'Ode to Evening' (1746) is composed in unrhymed lyrical stanzas derived from Milton's translation of Horace, creating an atmospheric pre-Romantic twilight mood.
Statement II: His 'Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegoric Subjects' (1746) celebrated personified abstractions such as Fear, Pity, and Simplicity with visionary intensity.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. William Collins was a seminal pre-Romantic lyricist whose visionary personifications and musical syntax deeply influenced the Romantic poets.

items.title: Quiz Q#141 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Adam Smith:
Statement I: In 'The Theory of Moral Sentiments' (1759), Adam Smith developed the moral concept of 'sympathy' and posited an internal 'impartial spectator' as the judge of human conduct.

Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true

items.title: Quiz Q#143 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Edmund Burke:
Statement I: In 'A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful' (1757), Edmund Burke linked the Sublime to sensations of terror, obscurity, and vastness.
Statement II: Burke's 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790) mounted a passionate defense of hereditary monarchy, prescriptive rights, and organic social stability against abstract radicalism.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Edmund Burke's aesthetic theory profoundly influenced Romanticism, while his 1790 treatise established modern philosophical conservatism and sparked the Revolutionary Controversy.

items.title: Quiz Q#144 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Cowper:
Statement I: William Cowper's 'The Task' (1785) is a major six-book poem in blank verse combining intimate domestic reflection, praise of rural retirement, and fierce anti-slavery conviction.
Statement II: Cowper's tragic late lyric 'The Castaway' (1799) uses the drowning of an 18th-century mariner as an agonizing metaphor for the poet's own conviction of spiritual damnation.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. William Cowper was the foremost pre-Romantic poet of evangelical devotion, domestic quietude, and psychological anguish.

items.title: Quiz Q#145 · Thomas Paine
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Paine
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Thomas Paine:
Statement I: Thomas Paine's 'Common Sense' (January 1776) utilized plain, persuasive language to rally American colonists toward an immediate declaration of independence from Britain.
Statement II: In 'Rights of Man' (1791–1792), Paine defended the principles of the French Revolution against Edmund Burke, arguing for universal natural rights and representative democracy.

Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true

items.title: Quiz Q#146 · James Boswell
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Boswell

Given below are two statements regarding James Boswell:
Statement I: James Boswell's 'The Life of Samuel Johnson' (1791) set a new standard for literary biography through dramatic dialogue, extensive letters, and verbatim conversational records.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

items.title: Quiz Q#149 · Thomas Chatterton

Statement I: Thomas Chatterton composed poems in forged pseudo-Middle English verse, falsely attributing them to a fictional 15th-century Bristol monk named Thomas Rowley.

Both Statement I and Statement II are true

items.title: Quiz Q#150 · William Godwin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Godwin
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Godwin:
Statement I: William Godwin's 'An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice' (1793) articulated a foundational philosophy of philosophical anarchism, rejecting government coercion in favor of human reason.
Statement II: In 'Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams' (1794), Godwin dramatized his political theories through a psychological thriller depicting the aristocratic tyranny of Falkland.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Godwin's philosophical treatise in 1793 and subsequent 1794 novel exercised immense intellectual influence over the first and second generation Romantic poets.

items.title: Quiz Q#151 · William Blake
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Blake
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Blake:
Statement I: William Blake's 'Songs of Innocence' (1789) and 'Songs of Experience' (1794) were printed using his proprietary method of illuminated copper-plate relief etching.
Statement II: In 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell' (1790), Blake subverted Swedenborgian morality with the 'Proverbs of Hell', asserting that 'Without Contraries is no progression'.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true

items.title: Quiz Q#152 · Mary Wollstonecraft
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Mary Wollstonecraft
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Mary Wollstonecraft:
Statement I: Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Men' (1790) was the very first published rebuttal to Edmund Burke's 'Reflections on the Revolution in France'.
Statement II: In 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792), Wollstonecraft argued that women's apparent moral and intellectual weaknesses resulted from deficient social conditioning and education.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Wollstonecraft's 1790 and 1792 treatises established her as a pioneering Enlightenment feminist and democratic thinker during the British Revolutionary Controversy.

items.title: Quiz Q#153 · Robert Burns
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Robert Burns
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Robert Burns:
Statement I: Robert Burns's 'Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect' (the 1786 Kilmarnock edition) established his fame as Scotland's national bard through poems like 'To a Mouse'.
Statement II: Burns's 1791 mock-heroic narrative poem 'Tam o' Shanter' is written in octosyllabic rhyming couplets and depicts an inebriated farmer stumbling upon a witches' dance at Alloway Kirk.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Robert Burns revitalized Scots vernacular poetry, combining folklore, political radicalism, and exquisite lyricism across his Kilmarnock poems and 'Tam o' Shanter'.

items.title: Quiz Q#154 · Ann Radcliffe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Ann Radcliffe
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Ann Radcliffe:
Statement I: Ann Radcliffe's 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' (1794) established the conventions of Gothic romance through Emily St. Aubert's imprisonment in the Apennine castle of the sinister Montoni.
Statement II: Radcliffe famously distinguished between 'terror' (which expands the soul and awakens faculties) and 'horror' (which contracts and annihilates them), employing the technique of the explained supernatural.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Ann Radcliffe was the supreme architect of 1790s Gothic fiction, combining sublime landscape descriptions with the psychological technique of terror and rationally explained mysteries.

items.title: Quiz Q#155 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan

options: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
items.explanation: Christian is a prominent figure in John Bunyan's The Pilgrim’s Progress, characterized as the pilgrim who leaves the city of destruction.

items.title: Quiz Q#156 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Flee from the wrath to come"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Bunyan's The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678).

items.title: Quiz Q#157 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan
items.stem: Which 1678 spiritual allegory by John Bunyan, composed largely during his imprisonment and framed as a dream vision, depicts Christian’s perilous journey carrying a burden from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City?
options: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
items.explanation: John Bunyan's masterwork 'The Pilgrim's Progress' was published in 1678 (Part II in 1684). Written as an allegorical dream narrative, it follows Christian through landmark allegorical locations such as the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, and the Valley of the Shadow of Death.

items.title: Quiz Q#158 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Bunyan does the character of Shaddai (The king who built Mansoul, standing for God) appear?
options: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
items.explanation: Shaddai is a prominent figure in John Bunyan's The Holy War, characterized as the king who built mansoul, standing for god.

items.title: Quiz Q#159 · John Bunyan
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Bunyan
items.stem: Which 1682 religious allegory by John Bunyan dramatizes the spiritual conflict for the soul of humanity through the siege of the metaphorical town of Mansoul by the giant Diabolus?
options: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
items.explanation: In 'The Holy War' (1682), John Bunyan allegorizes Christian salvation as the military defense and recapture of the fortress-town of Mansoul, whose gates correspond to human sensory organs such as Eye-gate and Ear-gate.

items.title: Quiz Q#160 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Crites (Defends ancient drama. He is based on Sir Robert Howard) appear?
items.explanation: Crites is a prominent figure in John Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy, characterized as defends ancient drama. he is based on sir robert howard.

items.title: Quiz Q#161 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The largest and most comprehensive soul"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668).

items.title: Quiz Q#162 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1668 critical dialogue by John Dryden presents a debate on the River Thames among four speakers (Crites, Eugenius, Lisideius, and Neander) evaluating classical, modern, French, and English theatre?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'An Essay of Dramatic Poesy' (1668) uses the persona of Neander (Dryden himself) to champion English Renaissance drama—especially William Shakespeare and Ben Jonson—while debating dramatic unities and rhymed verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#163 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Montezuma (The emperor of Mexico, whose kingdom falls to Spain) appear?
items.explanation: Montezuma is a prominent figure in John Dryden's The Indian Emperor, characterized as the emperor of mexico, whose kingdom falls to spain.

items.title: Quiz Q#164 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1667 heroic play by John Dryden, written in rhymed heroic couplets as a sequel to Sir Robert Howard's 'The Indian Queen', dramatizes the Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire under Cortez and Montezuma?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'The Indian Emperor, or the Conquest of Mexico by the Spaniards' (1667) was his first major theatrical triumph, written entirely in heroic couplets and establishing the conventions of Restoration heroic drama.

items.title: Quiz Q#165 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Rhodophil (A husband who is bored with marriage) appear?
items.explanation: Rhodophil is a prominent figure in John Dryden's Marriage à-la-Mode, characterized as a husband who is bored with marriage.

items.title: Quiz Q#166 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Why should a foolish marriage vow"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's Marriage à-la-Mode (1673).

items.title: Quiz Q#167 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1673 Restoration comedy by John Dryden combines a witty prose comedy of manners featuring the bored married couple Rhodophil and Doralice with a high heroic verse romance set in Sicily?
items.explanation: Dryden's 'Marriage à-la-Mode' (1673) is renowned for its dual plot: a cynical, witty prose comedy exploring fashionable marital boredom and swapping, paired with a romantic heroic plot composed in rhymed and blank verse.

items.title: Quiz Q#168 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Aureng-Zebe (The loyal son, based loosely on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb) appear?
items.explanation: Aureng-Zebe is a prominent figure in John Dryden's Aureng-Zebe, characterized as the loyal son, based loosely on the mughal emperor aurangzeb.

items.title: Quiz Q#169 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"When I consider life, 'tis all a cheat"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's Aureng-Zebe (1676).

items.title: Quiz Q#170 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1676 tragedy by John Dryden, based loosely on the contemporary succession struggles of the Mughal dynasty in India, marked his final play written in rhymed heroic couplets?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'Aureng-Zebe' (1676) is his last and finest rhymed heroic tragedy, dramatizing court rivalry in Agra and containing the iconic speech on life: 'When I consider life, 'tis all a cheat...'

items.title: Quiz Q#171 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Marc Antony (The Roman leader who chooses Cleopatra over Rome) appear?
items.explanation: Marc Antony is a prominent figure in John Dryden's All for Love, characterized as the roman leader who chooses cleopatra over rome.

items.title: Quiz Q#172 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Errors, like straws, upon the surface flow"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's All for Love (1678).

items.title: Quiz Q#173 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1678 tragedy by John Dryden, written in unrhymed blank verse to replace rhymed couplets, retells the tragic downfall of Antony and Cleopatra within the strict classical unities of time, place, and action?
items.explanation: In 'All for Love; or, The World Well Lost' (1678), John Dryden abandoned heroic rhyme for Shakespearean blank verse, compressing the sprawling scope of Shakespeare's 'Antony and Cleopatra' into a single day and single setting in Alexandria.

items.title: Quiz Q#174 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of David (The king in the poem, standing for Charles II) appear?
items.explanation: David is a prominent figure in John Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel, characterized as the king in the poem, standing for charles ii.

items.title: Quiz Q#175 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"In pious times, ere priestcraft did begin"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel (1681).

items.title: Quiz Q#176 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1681 political verse satire in heroic couplets by John Dryden uses the biblical rebellion of King David's son to allegorize the contemporary Exclusion Crisis, satirizing the Earl of Shaftesbury and the Duke of Monmouth?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'Absalom and Achitophel' (1681) is one of the greatest verse satires in English literature, defending King Charles II (David) while ruthlessly characterizing Shaftesbury as Achitophel and Buckingham as Zimri.

items.title: Quiz Q#177 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of Flecknoe (Richard Flecknoe, the aging king of dullness) appear?
items.explanation: Flecknoe is a prominent figure in John Dryden's Mac Flecknoe, characterized as richard flecknoe, the aging king of dullness.

items.title: Quiz Q#178 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"All human things are subject to decay"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Dryden's Mac Flecknoe (1682).

items.title: Quiz Q#179 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1682 mock-heroic verse satire by John Dryden crowns his literary adversary Thomas Shadwell as the undisputed heir to the realm of Non-sense and literary dullness?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'Mac Flecknoe' (1682) pioneered the English mock-heroic satire in heroic couplets, depicting the abdication of the dull poet Richard Flecknoe in favor of Shadwell, who 'alone, was he / By nature frame'd to stand for dullness and stupidity.'

items.title: Quiz Q#180 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Dryden does the character of The lay speaker (A Church of England believer who is not a priest. The title means a layman's faith) appear?

items.title: Quiz Q#181 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem:

"Dim, as the borrow'd beams of moon"
