items.title: Quiz Q#182 · John Dryden
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Dryden
items.stem: Which 1682 philosophical poem in heroic couplets by John Dryden offers a layman's rational defense of the Church of England against both Deism and Roman Catholic papal authority?
items.explanation: John Dryden's 'Religio Laici, or A Layman's Faith' (1682) defends the moderate Anglican via media using clear, unadorned heroic couplets, opening with the famous comparison of reason to the borrowed light of the moon and stars.

items.title: Quiz Q#183 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Locke does the character of John Locke (The writer, addressing a friend on toleration) appear?
items.explanation: John Locke is a prominent figure in John Locke's A Letter Concerning Toleration, characterized as the writer, addressing a friend on toleration.

items.title: Quiz Q#184 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"everyone is orthodox to himself"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Locke's A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689).

items.title: Quiz Q#185 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: Which 1689 treatise by John Locke, originally composed in Latin as 'Epistola de Tolerantia', argues for the strict separation of civil magistrate powers from ecclesiastical affairs?
items.explanation: John Locke's 'A Letter Concerning Toleration' (1689) asserts that religious belief cannot be coerced by state force, establishing the principle that civil governments exist solely to protect life, liberty, and property.

items.title: Quiz Q#186 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Locke does the character of John Locke (The philosopher arguing in his own voice) appear?
items.explanation: John Locke is a prominent figure in John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, characterized as the philosopher arguing in his own voice.

items.title: Quiz Q#187 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"white paper, void of all characters"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689).

items.title: Quiz Q#188 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: Which monumental 1689 philosophical work by John Locke rejects Cartesian innate ideas and posits that the human mind at birth is a 'tabula rasa' (blank slate) shaped exclusively by sensation and reflection?
items.explanation: John Locke's 'An Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) laid the foundation of British empiricism, arguing that all human knowledge originates in sensory experience and internal mental reflection.

items.title: Quiz Q#189 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Locke does the character of John Locke (The unnamed author of the two treatises) appear?
items.explanation: John Locke is a prominent figure in John Locke's Two Treatises of Government, characterized as the unnamed author of the two treatises.

items.title: Quiz Q#190 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"no one ought to harm another"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689).

items.title: Quiz Q#191 · John Locke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Locke
items.stem: Which foundational 1689 political treatise by John Locke refutes Sir Robert Filmer’s patriarchal divine right of kings in its first part, and establishes the social contract theory and natural rights in its second part?
items.explanation: Locke's 'Two Treatises of Government' (1689) justified the Glorious Revolution by arguing that sovereignty resides in the people, who enter a social contract to secure their natural rights to life, liberty, and property.

items.title: Quiz Q#192 · George Etherege
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · George Etherege
items.stem: In which landmark work by George Etherege does the character of Dorimant (The witty rake at the center of the love plots) appear?
options: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
items.explanation: Dorimant is a prominent figure in George Etherege's The Man of Mode, characterized as the witty rake at the center of the love plots.

items.title: Quiz Q#193 · George Etherege
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · George Etherege
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"He is indeed the pattern of modern foppery"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in George Etherege's The Man of Mode (1676).

items.title: Quiz Q#194 · George Etherege
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · George Etherege
items.stem: Which quintessential 1676 Restoration comedy of manners by Sir George Etherege, subtitled 'Sir Fopling Flutter', contrasts the sophisticated rakish wit of Dorimant with the absurd Frenchified pretensions of the titular fop?
options: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
items.explanation: George Etherege's 'The Man of Mode' (1676) defined Restoration social comedy through the amoral charms of Dorimant (widely believed to be based on the Earl of Rochester) and the foolish vanity of Sir Fopling Flutter.

items.title: Quiz Q#195 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: In which landmark work by Aphra Behn does the character of Silvia (A young woman based on Lady Henrietta Berkeley) appear?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Silvia is a prominent figure in Aphra Behn's Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister, characterized as a young woman based on lady henrietta berkeley.

items.title: Quiz Q#196 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The Amours of Philander and Silvia"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Aphra Behn's Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister (1684).

items.title: Quiz Q#197 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Which groundbreaking 1684 epistolary prose work by Aphra Behn, considered one of the earliest novels in English literature, dramatizes the scandalous romance of Silvia and Philander against the backdrop of the Monmouth Rebellion?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Aphra Behn's three-part novel 'Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister' (1684–1687) pioneered epistolary psychological fiction, blending erotic intrigue with political satire of Whig conspiracies.

items.title: Quiz Q#198 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: In which landmark work by Aphra Behn does the character of Willmore (The rover, a witty English captain who will not stay constant) appear?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Willmore is a prominent figure in Aphra Behn's The Rover, characterized as the rover, a witty english captain who will not stay constant.

items.title: Quiz Q#199 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Which popular 1677 comedy of intrigue by Aphra Behn, subtitled 'The Banish’d Cavaliers' and set during Carnival in Naples, centers on the dashing English privateer Captain Willmore and the wealthy courtezan Angellica Bianca?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Aphra Behn's 'The Rover' (1677), adapted from Thomas Killigrew's 'Thomaso', explores female sexual agency, commodification of women in marriage, and witty rakish adventures during the English Interregnum.

items.title: Quiz Q#200 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: In which landmark work by Aphra Behn does the character of Marcella (A young woman who loves Fillamour and pretends to be Euphemia) appear?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Marcella is a prominent figure in Aphra Behn's The Feigned Courtesans, characterized as a young woman who loves fillamour and pretends to be euphemia.

items.title: Quiz Q#201 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Which author wrote the 1679 Restoration comedy of intrigue subtitled 'A Night’s Intrigue' and featuring 'The Feigned Courtesans'?
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Aphra Behn's The Feigned Courtesans (1679).

items.title: Quiz Q#202 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Which 1679 Restoration comedy of intrigue by Aphra Behn, dedicated to Nell Gwyn and subtitled 'A Night’s Intrigue', follows two virtuous sisters who disguise themselves as high-class courtesans in Rome to escape arranged marriages?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: In Aphra Behn's 'The Feigned Courtesans' (1679), Marcella and Cornelia flee arranged domestic confinements by masquerading as Roman courtesans, exploring female resourcefulness and witty romantic entanglements.

items.title: Quiz Q#203 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: In which landmark work by Aphra Behn does the character of Oroonoko (Caesar) (A prince of Coramantien who is enslaved in Surinam) appear?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Oroonoko (Caesar) is a prominent figure in Aphra Behn's Oroonoko, characterized as a prince of coramantien who is enslaved in surinam.

items.title: Quiz Q#204 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Trophies of her Father's Victories"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Aphra Behn's Oroonoko (1688).

items.title: Quiz Q#205 · Aphra Behn
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Which landmark 1688 novella by Aphra Behn, subtitled 'The Royal Slave', recounts the tragic enslavement, noble rebellion, and brutal execution of an African prince in the English colony of Surinam?
options: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
items.explanation: Aphra Behn's 'Oroonoko: or, The Royal Slave' (1688) combines first-person travel narrative with heroic romance, presenting a sympathetic portrayal of the Coramantien prince Oroonoko (Caesar) and his beloved Imoinda.

items.title: Quiz Q#206 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem: In which landmark work by William Wycherley does the character of Horner (A rake who pretends he cannot love women) appear?
items.explanation: Horner is a prominent figure in William Wycherley's The Country Wife, characterized as a rake who pretends he cannot love women.

items.title: Quiz Q#207 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"He's a fool that marries"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Wycherley's The Country Wife (1675).

items.title: Quiz Q#208 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem: Which biting 1675 Restoration comedy by William Wycherley features the notorious rake Harry Horner feigning sexual impotence to gain unrestricted access to married women, including Margery Pinchwife?
items.explanation: William Wycherley's 'The Country Wife' (1675) is renowned for its scathing satire of London hypocrisy, sexual opportunism, and the famous double-entendre 'china scene'.

items.title: Quiz Q#209 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem: In which landmark work by William Wycherley does the character of Captain Manly (A blunt sailor who thinks he alone speaks the truth) appear?
items.explanation: Captain Manly is a prominent figure in William Wycherley's The Plain Dealer, characterized as a blunt sailor who thinks he alone speaks the truth.

items.title: Quiz Q#210 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I weigh the man, not his title"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Wycherley's The Plain Dealer (1677).

items.title: Quiz Q#211 · William Wycherley
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Wycherley
items.stem: Which 1676 satirical play by William Wycherley, adapted from Molière's 'Le Misanthrope', follows the fiercely misanthropic naval captain Manly as he navigates court corruption and betrayal?
items.explanation: In 'The Plain Dealer' (1676), Wycherley critiques legal and social corruption through Captain Manly, whose unbending honesty exposes the greed of his mistress Olivia and the loyalty of the disguised Fidelia.

items.title: Quiz Q#212 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem: In which landmark work by Thomas Otway does the character of Monimia (The orphan ward whom both brothers love) appear?
items.explanation: Monimia is a prominent figure in Thomas Otway's The Orphan, characterized as the orphan ward whom both brothers love.

items.title: Quiz Q#213 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Woman, the fountain of all human frailty!"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Otway's The Orphan (1680).

items.title: Quiz Q#214 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem: Which 1680 Restoration tragedy in blank verse by Thomas Otway, subtitled 'The Unhappy Marriage', dramatizes the catastrophic rivalry between twin brothers Castalio and Polydore for the love of the ward Monimia?
items.explanation: Thomas Otway's 'The Orphan' (1680) shifted tragic focus from grand political statecraft to intimate domestic pathos, establishing the influential convention of the suffering, innocent heroine.

items.title: Quiz Q#215 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem: In which landmark work by Thomas Otway does the character of Jaffeir (A poor gentleman torn between the plot and his wife) appear?
items.explanation: Jaffeir is a prominent figure in Thomas Otway's Venice Preserved, characterized as a poor gentleman torn between the plot and his wife.

items.title: Quiz Q#216 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"O woman! lovely woman!"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Otway's Venice Preserved (1682).

items.title: Quiz Q#217 · Thomas Otway
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Thomas Otway
items.stem: Which 1682 blank verse tragedy by Thomas Otway, subtitled 'A Plot Discover’d', depicts the moral agony of Jaffeir, torn between his conspirator friend Pierre and his devoted wife Belvidera?
items.explanation: Thomas Otway's 'Venice Preserv'd' (1682) is considered the greatest tragic drama of the Restoration, reflecting the political anxieties of the Popish Plot while depicting tragic domestic and political ruin.

items.title: Quiz Q#218 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: In which landmark work by Daniel Defoe does the character of H. F. (The saddler who tells the story and stays in the city) appear?
options: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: H. F. is a prominent figure in Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year, characterized as the saddler who tells the story and stays in the city.

items.title: Quiz Q#219 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The plague was returned again in Holland"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year (1722).

items.title: Quiz Q#220 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: Which 1722 prose work by Daniel Defoe reconstructs the 1665 Great Plague of London with journalistic precision through the first-person perspective of an observant saddler identified only as 'H. F.'?
options: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Daniel Defoe's 'A Journal of the Plague Year' (1722) uses statistical records, bills of mortality, and vivid eyewitness anecdotes to pioneer documentary realism in English prose fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#221 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: In which landmark work by Daniel Defoe does the character of The ironic speaker (A pretended speaker who calls for harsh punishments) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: The ironic speaker is a prominent figure in Daniel Defoe's The Shortest Way with the Dissenters, characterized as a pretended speaker who calls for harsh punishments.

items.title: Quiz Q#222 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The shortest way with the Dissenters"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Daniel Defoe's The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702).

items.title: Quiz Q#223 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: Which 1702 satirical pamphlet by Daniel Defoe mimicked the extreme rhetoric of High Church Tories by proposing the violent eradication of religious nonconformists, leading to Defoe's arrest and pillorying?
options: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: In 'The Shortest Way with the Dissenters' (1702), Defoe adopted an ironic persona so convincing that both High Church Anglicans and Dissenters initially took it literally, causing scandal when his authorship was revealed.

items.title: Quiz Q#224 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: In which landmark work by Daniel Defoe does the character of Robinson Crusoe (A restless English sailor who lives alone on the island) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Robinson Crusoe is a prominent figure in Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, characterized as a restless english sailor who lives alone on the island.

items.title: Quiz Q#225 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I was born in the year 1632"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719).

items.title: Quiz Q#226 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: Which 1719 foundational English novel by Daniel Defoe chronicles the survival, resourcefulness, and spiritual transformation of an English castaway shipwrecked for 28 years on a deserted Caribbean island?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Daniel Defoe's 'Robinson Crusoe' (1719) is often heralded as the first modern English novel, celebrated for its economic individualism, Puritan spiritual introspection, and realistic domestic detail.

items.title: Quiz Q#227 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: In which landmark work by Daniel Defoe does the character of Moll Flanders (The narrator, a thief and many times a wife, born in Newgate) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Moll Flanders is a prominent figure in Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders, characterized as the narrator, a thief and many times a wife, born in newgate.

items.title: Quiz Q#228 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I would be a gentlewoman"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders (1722).

items.title: Quiz Q#229 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: Which 1722 episodic novel by Daniel Defoe traces the life of a resourceful woman born in Newgate Prison who survives through five marriages, twelve years of thievery, and transportation to Virginia?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Defoe's 'Moll Flanders' (1722) combines the conventions of the picaresque and criminal confession narrative to explore social mobility, economic survival, and female agency in early modern London.

items.title: Quiz Q#230 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: In which landmark work by Daniel Defoe does the character of Roxana (The narrator, a courtesan also called the Fortunate Mistress) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Roxana is a prominent figure in Daniel Defoe's Roxana, characterized as the narrator, a courtesan also called the fortunate mistress.

items.title: Quiz Q#231 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: "The Fortunate Mistress" is the celebrated subtitle of the 1724 novel 'Roxana', written by which author?
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Daniel Defoe's Roxana (1724).

items.title: Quiz Q#232 · Daniel Defoe
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Daniel Defoe
items.stem: Which 1724 novel by Daniel Defoe, subtitled 'The Fortunate Mistress', explores the moral corruption, financial ambition, and eventual psychological ruin of a courtesan who abandons her children for wealth?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
items.explanation: Defoe's final novel 'Roxana: The Fortunate Mistress' (1724) is a darker study of guilt and ambition than 'Moll Flanders', ending with the protagonist haunted by the unrepented consequences of her deceit.

items.title: Quiz Q#233 · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester does the character of The Speaker (A cynical court wit who attacks pride in reason) appear?
options: A Satire against Reason and Mankind
items.explanation: The Speaker is a prominent figure in John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester's A Satire against Reason and Mankind, characterized as a cynical court wit who attacks pride in reason.

items.title: Quiz Q#234 · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Who is so proud of being rational"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester's A Satire against Reason and Mankind (1679).

items.title: Quiz Q#235 · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
items.stem: Which biting 1674 verse satire by John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester, influenced by Hobbes and Boileau, argues that human reason is inferior to animal instinct because men use intellect to betray one another?
options: A Satire against Reason and Mankind
items.explanation: Rochester's 'A Satire against Reason and Mankind' (1674) employs crisp heroic couplets to attack scholastic philosophy and celebrate sensory experience over abstract metaphysical delusion.

items.title: Quiz Q#236 · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.stem: In which landmark work by Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680) does the character of Sir Hudibras (A Presbyterian knight, pedantic and absurdly brave) appear?
items.explanation: Sir Hudibras is a prominent figure in Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)'s Hudibras, characterized as a presbyterian knight, pedantic and absurdly brave.

items.title: Quiz Q#237 · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"He that complies against his will"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)'s Hudibras (1663).

items.title: Quiz Q#238 · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.stem: Which celebrated Restoration verse satire by Samuel Butler burlesques Presbyterian and Independent religious hypocrisy through the quixotic misadventures of a pedantic knight and his squire Ralpho?
items.explanation: Samuel Butler's 'Hudibras' (published in three parts between 1663 and 1678) coined 'Hudibrastic verse'—doggerel octosyllabic rhyming couplets featuring comic, grotesque, and polysyllabic rhymes.

items.title: Quiz Q#239 · Samuel Pepys
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Pepys
items.stem: In which landmark work by Samuel Pepys does the character of Samuel Pepys (The diarist, Clerk of the Acts and later a navy secretary) appear?
items.explanation: Samuel Pepys is a prominent figure in Samuel Pepys's Diary, characterized as the diarist, clerk of the acts and later a navy secretary.

items.title: Quiz Q#240 · Samuel Pepys
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Pepys
items.stem: Which private shorthand journal kept between 1660 and 1669 provides an unparalleled eyewitness chronicle of the Restoration, the Great Plague, the Great Fire of London, and the Dutch Wars?
items.explanation: Samuel Pepys's 'Diary', transcribed from Thomas Shelton's shorthand in the 19th century, offers an extraordinarily frank and vivid personal and historical portrait of early Restoration London.

items.title: Quiz Q#241 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Vanbrugh does the character of Loveless (A husband who slips back from reform) appear?
items.explanation: Loveless is a prominent figure in John Vanbrugh's The Relapse, characterized as a husband who slips back from reform.

items.title: Quiz Q#242 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem: Which witty 1696 Restoration comedy by Sir John Vanbrugh, subtitled 'Virtue in Danger', was written as an irreverent sequel and cynical rebuttal to Colley Cibber’s sentimental 'Love’s Last Shift'?
items.explanation: Vanbrugh's 'The Relapse' (1696) features Lord Foppington (formerly Sir Novelty Fashion) and demonstrates that Cibber's reformed libertine Loveless promptly relapses into infidelity upon arriving in London.

items.title: Quiz Q#243 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Vanbrugh does the character of Sir John Brute (A coarse husband who hates married life) appear?
items.explanation: Sir John Brute is a prominent figure in John Vanbrugh's The Provoked Wife, characterized as a coarse husband who hates married life.

items.title: Quiz Q#244 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"What cloying meat is love"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Vanbrugh's The Provoked Wife (1697).

items.title: Quiz Q#245 · John Vanbrugh
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Vanbrugh
items.stem: Which 1697 comedy by Sir John Vanbrugh examines the misery of an incompatible marriage, starring the drunken brute Sir John Brute and his neglected, tempted spouse Lady Brute?
items.explanation: Vanbrugh's 'The Provoked Wife' (1697) challenged conventional domestic assumptions, earning fierce criticism in Jeremy Collier's 1698 anti-theatrical tract 'A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage'.

items.title: Quiz Q#246 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem: In which landmark work by Matthew Prior does the character of Bayes (A foolish poet who reads the mouse poem. He stands for Dryden) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d
items.explanation: Bayes is a prominent figure in Matthew Prior's The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d, characterized as a foolish poet who reads the mouse poem. he stands for dryden.

items.title: Quiz Q#247 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"A milk-white Mouse immortal and unchang'd"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Matthew Prior's The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d (1687).

items.title: Quiz Q#248 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem: Which 1687 verse parody by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu ridiculed John Dryden’s beast fable by re-enacting its religious debates as a dialogue between the City Mouse and the Country Mouse?
options: The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Subtitled 'To the Story of the Country-Mouse and the City-Mouse' (1687), this witty burlesque satirized Dryden's Catholic apologetics in 'The Hind and the Panther' by reducing high theological debate to barnyard squabbling.

items.title: Quiz Q#249 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem: In which landmark work by Matthew Prior does the character of Henry (The lover in Henry and Emma who tests the woman's loyalty) appear?
options: The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Henry is a prominent figure in Matthew Prior's Poems on Several Occasions, characterized as the lover in henry and emma who tests the woman's loyalty.

Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Here lies what once was Matthew Prior"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Matthew Prior's Poems on Several Occasions (1709).
